title: “The sugar is under 200”
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; treatment protocols and doses come from the hospital, not this case. The attending’s judgment comes first.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident co-managing surgical patients overnight at a tertiary hospital in Davao City. At 03:00 on Tuesday, the intern, Dr. Paolo Dizon, brings you an arterial blood gas from Mr. Arnel Velasco, 55, who has type 2 diabetes and heart failure. His cardiologist added a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor last year, which he buys out of pocket. Two days ago he had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy; he has barely eaten since and began vomiting last evening. He received an opioid injection for pain at 01:30 and is drowsy, breathing 18 times a minute.

The gas shows pH 7.15, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO₂) 30 mm Hg and bicarbonate 10 mmol/L. Sodium is 136 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL and albumin 3.0 g/dL.

n1.prompt: Read the gas. What is going on, and what do you do?

choices.text: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation; calculate the gaps before calling anyone.
choices.feedback: The compensation check fails: expected PaCO₂ is 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23, range 21 to 25 mm Hg, and his is 30. A pH below 7.2 also needs a call now, before the gaps.
choices.then: You redo the arithmetic and call the attending; the nurse watches his breathing closely.

choices.text: Metabolic acidosis with an added respiratory acidosis: expected PaCO₂ is 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 (21 to 25), and 30 is too high. With a pH below 7.2, call the attending now and have his breathing watched closely.
choices.feedback: Compensation never quite reaches normal, but a PaCO₂ above the expected range means ventilation is not keeping up, here plausibly from the opioid or tiring. If his breathing fails, the pH will fall sharply.

choices.text: A primary respiratory acidosis from the opioid; recheck the gas after breakfast.
choices.feedback: In acidemia, a low bicarbonate means a metabolic acidosis; a primary respiratory acidosis would raise the PaCO₂, not leave it at 30. Waiting five hours with a pH of 7.15 risks collapse.
choices.then: Dr. Dizon asks you to look again at the bicarbonate. You call the attending; the nurse watches his breathing closely.

choices.text: Start a bicarbonate infusion to correct the pH, and review in the morning.
choices.feedback: Bicarbonate treats the number, not the cause, and it adds sodium and can cause alkalosis. The urgent problems are a pH below 7.2 and breathing that is not keeping up.
choices.then: You hold the bicarbonate and call the attending; the nurse watches his breathing closely.

n2.prompt: Now the electrolytes. What do they show?

choices.feedback: Vomiting removes acid and causes metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis. And the gap is not normal: 136 − (100 + 10) = 26 mmol/L.
choices.then: You recalculate the gap and correct it for albumin.

choices.text: Anion gap 26 mmol/L: a high-gap acidosis.
choices.feedback: Correct, but his albumin is 3.0 g/dL. Each 1 g/dL fall lowers the gap by about 2.5 mmol/L, so make the correction a habit; in a patient with a lower albumin it can unmask a gap that looks normal.
choices.then: You correct it to about 28.5 mmol/L and list the causes.

choices.text: Anion gap 136 − (100 + 10) = 26 mmol/L; corrected for an albumin of 3.0 g/dL, about 28.5. A high-gap acidosis: check ketones, lactate, kidney failure and toxins.
choices.feedback: Albumin carries most of the normal gap, so a low albumin hides part of a rise. The rise in the gap (about 14) roughly matches the fall in bicarbonate (about 14), so there is no strong sign of a second metabolic disorder, keeping in mind that the ratio varies.

n3.scene: The results return: beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.4 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. His creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL, and his wife says he drinks no alcohol. The surgical resident says: “The sugar is under 200. It can’t be diabetic ketoacidosis.”
n3.prompt: What is your diagnosis and next step?

choices.text: Not diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) with a glucose below 200; observe and repeat the gas at 08:00.
choices.feedback: The 2024 consensus accepts a known history of diabetes in place of a glucose of 200 mg/dL or more, precisely to capture ketoacidosis with a near-normal glucose. He meets every criterion, and waiting four hours with a pH of 7.15 is dangerous.
choices.then: The attending reviews the numbers by phone and confirms DKA. The hospital DKA protocol starts and the SGLT2 inhibitor is held.

vitals.order: DKA protocol with attending; SGLT2 inhibitor held

choices.text: Probably DKA; wait for the endocrinologist at 09:00 to confirm before starting treatment.
choices.feedback: The criteria are met now, and a five-hour delay leaves a pH of 7.15 untreated. Start the protocol with the attending tonight and involve the endocrinologist in the morning.
choices.then: You call the attending, who starts the DKA protocol now; the SGLT2 inhibitor is held.

vitals.order: DKA protocol with attending; SGLT2 inhibitor held

choices.text: Starvation ketosis; give dextrose and let him eat when he is ready.
choices.feedback: Starvation ketosis does not drive the bicarbonate down to 10 mmol/L. A beta-hydroxybutyrate of 5.4 mmol/L with a pH below 7.3 in a man with diabetes is DKA.
choices.then: The attending confirms DKA by phone; the protocol starts and the SGLT2 inhibitor is held.

vitals.order: DKA protocol with attending; SGLT2 inhibitor held

choices.text: DKA by the 2024 consensus criteria (known diabetes, beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 mmol/L or more, pH below 7.3) with a near-normal glucose, linked to his SGLT2 inhibitor after surgery and fasting. Start the hospital DKA protocol with the attending and hold the SGLT2 inhibitor.
choices.feedback: SGLT2 inhibitors lower glucose through glycosuria, so a patient can be ketoacidotic with a glucose that looks reassuring, especially after surgery, fasting or acute illness. The anion gap and the glucose are no longer what defines DKA.

vitals.order: DKA protocol with attending; SGLT2 inhibitor held

n4.scene: Fifteen hours later he is alert, and he has received several liters of 0.9% saline. The gas shows pH 7.31, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg and bicarbonate 15 mmol/L; sodium is 140 mmol/L and chloride 115 mmol/L. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is 0.6 mmol/L. The nurse asks whether the DKA is “still not fixed,” and Dr. Dizon suggests a urine anion gap to look for renal tubular acidosis.
n4.prompt: How do you read this gas?

choices.text: The ketoacidosis has resolved: the gap is 140 − (115 + 15) = 10 and the ketones are low. What remains is a normal-gap acidosis from the chloride in the saline. Tell the attending so the plan can be reviewed.
choices.feedback: Saline carries equal sodium and chloride, more chloride than plasma; large volumes lower the strong ion difference and the bicarbonate. Now the bicarbonate has fallen more than the gap explains, which is the delta pattern of an added normal-gap acidosis.

vitals.order: Gap closed; hyperchloremia reported to attending

choices.text: Send a urine anion gap to look for renal tubular acidosis.
choices.feedback: The urine anion gap misleads when ketones and other unmeasured anions are in the urine, as they are after DKA. The story already explains the chloride.
choices.then: You recalculate the anion gap and report the hyperchloremia to the attending.

vitals.order: Gap closed; hyperchloremia reported to attending

choices.text: The DKA is getting worse because the bicarbonate is still 15; intensify the protocol.
choices.feedback: The anion gap has closed to 140 − (115 + 15) = 10, and the ketones have cleared. The low bicarbonate now has a different cause, and intensifying ketoacidosis treatment does not fix it.
choices.then: You recalculate the gap and report the hyperchloremia to the attending.

vitals.order: Gap closed; hyperchloremia reported to attending

n5.scene: On day 4 he is eating, and his bicarbonate is 22 mmol/L. His wife asks whether he should go back on “the heart and sugar tablet.”
n5.prompt: What do you do about the SGLT2 inhibitor?

choices.text: Tell him to stop it permanently and never take it again.
choices.feedback: He takes it for diabetes and heart failure, uses for which these drugs are increasingly prescribed. A permanent stop is a decision for the attending and his cardiologist with him, not a discharge reflex.
choices.then: You discuss it with the attending, who asks his cardiologist to decide and asks you to teach the warning signs.

vitals.order: Diagnosis written; restart decision with attending and cardiologist

choices.text: Write the diagnosis, SGLT2 inhibitor-associated DKA with a near-normal glucose after surgery and fasting, in the discharge summary; leave the restart decision to the attending and his cardiologist; and teach him and his wife that ketoacidosis can occur with a normal sugar during fasting, vomiting or surgery, and when to come back.
choices.feedback: The next doctor needs to know why this happened, and the patient needs to recognize it early. Naming the drug and the setting makes the next episode less likely to be missed.

vitals.order: Diagnosis written; restart decision with attending and cardiologist

choices.text: Restart it at discharge as before; the episode is over.
choices.feedback: Nothing about his risk has been discussed or documented. If he fasts or vomits again, the same normal-looking glucose may hide the same ketoacidosis.
choices.then: The attending asks you to hold the restart decision for his cardiologist and to teach the warning signs.

vitals.order: Diagnosis written; restart decision with attending and cardiologist

end.title: Discharge
end.text: Mr. Velasco goes home on day 5. His discharge summary names the diagnosis and the setting, and his cardiologist will decide about the SGLT2 inhibitor at his clinic visit next week. His wife knows that vomiting, fast breathing or abdominal pain while he is not eating means a return to the hospital, even if his sugar reading looks normal.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Check compensation every time. A PaCO₂ above 1.5 × bicarbonate + 8 (±2) means an added respiratory acidosis; a pH below 7.2 means a call now.
  • Correct the anion gap for albumin, then ask: ketones, lactate, kidney failure, toxin.
  • DKA is defined by ketones and acidosis in a person with diabetes, not by a glucose above 200; ask about SGLT2 inhibitors in every unexplained high-gap acidosis.
  • As DKA resolves, watch the gap, not just the bicarbonate. A closed gap with a low bicarbonate after liters of saline is a chloride acidosis, and the urine anion gap misleads while ketones are in the urine.

See Step by step, The gaps and Special problems.
